Athens.
Special to the Herald.
Athens, March, 13.—A negro by the name of Elbert Rogers, for some time past residing at Brownsboro, this county, stole a orse from a farmer by the name of Chas. Patton, living in this neighborhood, a day or two ago and was traced through Athens west, by Deputy Sheriff Carver and Patton until, they came up with him at Cedar Creek, this county, and on yesterday brought him back to Athens and lodged him in jail, he being nearly dead, having received a pistol shot in the back, the ball passing into his stomach. On yesterday morning at daylight, he was dead, and a coroners jury decided that death was caused by a pistol ball by an unknown hand. The Probate court is in session. Farmers are busy, and business in town dull. Prospects are good for a crop this year.

Shreveport Times.]
Henry Solomon, who was confined in jail at Bellevue on the charge of stealing a mule from Mr. John J. Stockwell, and who escaped from jail on the night of the 10th instant with Jack Chapman, under sentence of death, was arrested Sunday afternoon by Deputy Sheriff John C. On last Tuesday night the parish jail at this place was set on fire by Henry Solomon, colored, incarcerated on the charge of mule stealing. The fire was first discovered by deputies R. E. Wyche, jr., and C. W. Edwards, who immediately gave the alarm, and other citizens promptly coming to their assistance the fire was extinguished before any serious damage could result from the work of the incendiary, otherwise there would undoubtedly have been quite a disastrous conflagration in our town.

Between 1 and 2 o'clock on the same night, 10 or 12 unknown persons entered the room of deputy sheriff, R. E. Wyche, jr., and forcibly took from him the keys of the jail. Yesterday morning the body of Henry Solomon was found hanging to the platform of the jail. An inquisition, taken before Dr. W. J. Mobley, Parish Coroner, returned the following verdict:

"We, the jury, after due inquiry and examination of witnesses summoned before us, find the deceased, Henry Solomon, came to his death by dislocation of neck, caused by hanging, by the hands of parties unknown to these jurors.
B. A. KELLY, Foreman.
J. J. DAVIS.
E. J. MCKILLIPS.
WASHINGTON ALLEN.
FRANK CAMPBELL.
R. E. Wyche, J., sworn before Coroner's jury, states:
"That he is deputy sheriff, and was so on the 24th January, 1882, and as such, he had charge of the keys of the parish jail of Bossier parish. That the deceased, Henry Solomon, was incarcerated in the Bossier parish jail, on the charge of male stealing; and that said deceased was in the upper west cell by himself, and was shackled to the floor, and also chained to the floor. A fire was discovered about 10½ o'clock P. M., by witness, in the cell in which the deceased was confined. The witness gave the alarm and entered the cell in company with C. W. Edwards, another deputy sheriff, and other parties. He found the deceased disengaged from the floor, and the chain was broken. He saw the door of trap which leads to lower cell in flames, and fire had burned through said door, and cinders and nails were dropping in lower cell, and the deceased, Henry Solomon, admitted that he set the jail on fire for the purpose of escaping. The destruction of entire building was in danger, and was saved by himself and the efforts of those who came to his aid, on his giving the alarm. After fire, they changed the prisoner from the upper east cell, and be afterwards returned in company with C. W. Edwards, and both retired. Between 1 and 2 A. M., Jan. 26, 1882, his room was entered by 10 or 12 unknown parties, who demanded of him the keys, and forcibly compelled him to give up the keys, by threatenings. He was sleeping at his father's residence—Mr. R. R. Wyche, Sr. Mr. C. W. Edwards and two colored men were sleeping in said same room—names of colored men being Thomas Paysinger and Sledge Bryant—who were sleeping on floor in same room by the fire. That the partitions

JUDGE LYNCH IN LOUISIANA.
A Horse Thief and Incendiary
Hanged from the Second Story of
the Jail.
SHREVEPORT, LA., January 26 — News of the hanging of a negro named Henry Solomon at Bellevue, Bossier parish, reached here last night. He was confined for horse stealing, and set fire to the building, which was discovered by the guards before it got under headway, otherwise much property would have been destroyed and lives lost. The fire occurred about midnight, and the body of Solomon was found hanging from the second story of the jail yesterday morning. There is no clue to those who took part in the hanging.
henry-solomon-bellevue-1882-01-26.A9: Henry Solomon, colored, who was confined in the parish jail of Bossier on the charge of mule stealing, attempted to make his escape by setting fire to the jail. The fire was extinguished before any serious damage was done. On the same night a number of unknown men entered the room of the deputy sheriff and demanded the jail keys. The next morning Henry Solomon was found hanging to the platform of the jail.
henry-solomon-bellevue-1882-01-26.A10:
MORE LYNCHING.
MORE LYNCHING.
The usually staid and law abiding parish of Bossier has been disgraced by a lynching affair. Tuesday night of last week a party of about a dozen men gained admission to the jailor's bedroom, obtained possession of the keys of the jail by threats, entered the prison and brought out Henry Solomon, a colored man, whom they hanged just outside the building. An inquest was held and, as usual, the jailor, his assistants and the prisoners incarcerated with Solomon all testified that they did not recognize any of the lynchers, though it does not even appear from the evidence, as reported by the Banner, that the law breakers were masked or disguised in any way.

Solomon had been imprisoned on a charge of mule stealing, and was thought to be a bad character, but it is not urged that he was ever convicted of any offense. During the night of the 10th inst., in company with one Jack Chapman, a white man convicted of murder and sentenced to death, Solomon broke out of jail and fled. The pair were subsequently captured and returned to prison. The night of the lynching the floor of the cell occupied by Solomon was found to be burning, and the prisoner is said to have acknowledged that he started the fire with the intention of effecting an escape. We presume this was the overt act that justified the lynchers, in their own estimation, in murdering a man who had never been convicted of any breach of law and was entitled to the legal presumption of innocence until proven guilty.

The Bossier Banner regrets the occurrence and says "such a method of inflicting justice is undoubtedly dangerous," but expresses "the candid belief that the legal quibbles and quirks so freely used in defense of criminals everywhere, now-a-days, is answerable for this state of affairs."

The excuse is a very weak one in this instance, for no attempt had yet been made under the forms of law to bring Solomon to an account for his alleged misdeeds. If the night-prowling jayhawkers were actuated by the fear that a criminal would escape punishment unless they inflicted it outside the pale of the law, why did they select a poor darkkey, never convicted of crime and only accused of stealing a mule, passing by a white murderer who had been duly tried and pronounced guilty and who is endeavoring to evade the penalty of his great crime—one of the most serious and infamous in the category of lawless deeds—by "legal quibbles and quirks?" Jake Chapman is prosecuting an appeal before the Supreme Court, and should any irregularity be discovered in the proceedings in his case, he will be granted a new trial and will stand the chance of securing an acquittal or of making a second and more successful attempt to escape by breaking jail and fleeing to parts unknown. If Solomon's effort to regain his liberty by flight is taken as a confession of guilt, the same assumption must apply in Chapman's case, even signifying the fact that the latter had been duly tried and convicted, while the former had never been accorded the right of a trial.

It certainly appears on the face of the record that the Bossier lynchers made a very marked distinction between white tweedle-dee and colored tweedle-dum, and in three out of every four instances of lynching in Louisiana the same tendency is to be observed. Notwithstanding the fact that the proportion of criminals who escape punishment in this State is fully three white to one colored, a considerable majority of those murdered by the outrageous methods of Judge Lynch are colored prisoners whose facilities for taking advantage of "legal quibbles and quirks" are far inferior to those of the white malefactor. It is a great pity for the credit of the State and its people, an example can not be made of some of these cowardly murderers who, under the pretense of punishing crime, violate the sacred rights of citizenship, break through the most valuable safeguards of society and place themselves on a level with the worst of malefactors that infest the country. We can imagine a state of affairs that would palliate and justify a resort to extra-judicial proceedings to restore good order and suppress crime, but no such condition exists in Louisiana or in Bossier parish, and there was no adequate warrant or justification for the application of mob law in the instance just noted.

Jack Chapman, colored, convicted of the murder of another colored man and sentenced by Judge Drew to be hanged at the September term of Bossier District Court, and now confined in our parish jail, will doubtless hang at an early day, the jugment of the lower Court having been recently affirmed by the Supreme Court. Following is a synopsis of the decision:

No. 8405—State of Louisiana vs. Jack Chapman.—Appeal from the District Court of Bossier Parish.—The power of the District Court to correct its minutes so as to make them conform to the truth is recognized and well settled in our jurisprudence. The fact that in passing a sentence of death on a criminal the District Judge fixes in his judgment the day and date of the execution—a duty devolving upon the Governor—does not vitiate the judgment or the trial, and will afford no relief to the defendant on appeal. That portion of the sentence will be considered as unwritten. The Supreme Court will not review the refusal of a new trial on a motion involving questions of law blended with facts, unless the grounds are incorporated in a bill of exceptions. State vs. Nelson, 32 A., 842, reaffirmed.

Austin.
Special to the Herald.
AUSTIN, January 3.—Shortly before midnight last night an ex-convict named Emmet McPhail, about 19 years old, was killed in the baglio of Sallie Daggett, under the following circumstances: Early in the night deceased and a companion named Jeff Ake, having assaulted a colored man, who, with his wife, was returning from church, Officer Watts, with William McLennan, whom he summoned to his assistance, searched and traced them to the baglio, where he found them in the wine-room. When the officer entered he told the men they were under arrest, whereupon they both drew their pistols. Watts knocked McPhail off the gallery and clinched with the other, who thereupon fired two shots, one of the balls striking Watts in the side, inflicting a slight wound. Seeing the other man about to fire, Watts ordered McLennan, who was unarmed, to take his (Watts') pistol and shoot him. McLennan obeyed, shooting the aggressor through the heart. Jeff Ake was then overpowered and taken to jail. A jury of inquest this morning returned a verdict of justifiable homicide. Jeff Ake is an ex-convict having been pardoned by the Governor while serving a term for horse-stealing. McPharl's penal servitude was for horse theft.
The Capitol Commissioners are busy. In view, if possible, of securing conditions acceptable to the Capitol Board, the meetings are strictly private and all parties are under the seal of secrecy. It is not thought that any concessions can be made by the State on the specifications. If no agreements can be reached the lands will be put up at sale.
No new case of small pox has been reported to-day.
The Manner farm of 250 acres, several miles northwest of the city, has been purchased by the government for $5,000.
ike-johnson-1882-01-02.A3:
SAD END.
AN UNKNOWN WHITE MAN
KILLED IN A BAGINO.
AN OFFICER WOUNDED IN
THE MELEE.
FULL STATEMENT OF THE TRAGIC AFFAIR.
Last night at about half past 10 o'clock it was reported on the streets that a man had been killed down in the first ward, at the house of ill-fame kept by Sallie Daggett. A reporter of the STATESMAN was there in a few minutes, and found the report to be true; also that police-man John Watts had wounded. The young man killed was an entire stranger, not one of the immense throng that visited the scene of the killing recognizing him. He was

A COW BOY,
about twenty years of age, and dressed in the usual garb worn by that class. Dr. Cummings, the city physician, was summoned by the marshal, but when he arrived the man was about drawing his expiring breath. He was shot near and lived only about half an hour after being struck by the fatal bullet. The ball was from a large-sized policeman's pistol, and delivered at close range.

THE PARTICULARS
of the shooting, as near as they could be gathered, are about as follows: In the early part of the night a colored man named Ike Johnson was on his way home from church in a wagon with his wife. When out near the north limits of the city, two white men on horseback rode up, one on either side, and commenced to whip his horses. He remonstrated with them, whereupon they drew their six-shooters and threatened to kill him. Afterwards the colored man came to the city and reported the case to Officer John Watts, of the police force, who went in search of the men. They were traced to the house of ill-fame kept by Sallie Daggett, in the first ward. Their horses were found fastened in front of the house, and the officer, ascertaining that the men were upon the inside, went in to arrest them, summoning Mr. William McLellan to assist him. The men were in the WINE ROOM,
to reach which it is necessary to pass out at the rear hall door and across a small portico. When the officer started in he met the two-men on this portico,
and laving a hand upon either one told
them they were under arrest. Without
a word both men

DREW THEIR PISTOLS.

The officer knocked one off the gallery and clinched with the other. The one in the grasp of the officer fired one, or may be two shots, one of the balls striking Mr. Watts in the side, inflicting a slight wound. The other man, who was knocked off the gallery, had in the meantime recovered himself and was in the act of shooting at the officer, when the latter directed Mr. McLellan, who was unarmed, to take his (the officer's)

PISTOL AND SHOOT HIM.

McLellan took the pistol as directed and fired twice, the second ball taking effect as described above. The other man, whose name is Jeff Ake, was finally overpowered and carried to the police station. He was afterwards delivered to Sheriff Creary and placed in jail.

A JURY OF INQUEST

was formed by Justice Gregg, who had been notified. The jury examined the body, but the taking of testimony was deferred until to-day. No one seemed to recognize the dead man. He had upon his person, besides some other trifling articles, such as tobacco, a pocket-book with no money in it, etc., a letter dated at Austin and directed to Clark & Chenoweth and signed

J. A. MCPHAIL.

The letter was not enclosed in an envelope, and contained no evidence of the locality of the parties to whom addressed. It is presumed the name signed to the letter is that of the dead man, but this of course is not certain. The letter asked for legal advice, and evidently the writer was charged with some crime somewhere and was either a fugitive from justice or was at liberty upon a bail bond.

JEFF AKE

is well known in this community, being a somewhat notorious chaacter. He was bardoned out of the penitentiary some time during the surummer by the governor, having been sent there, we believe, for horse stealing. A reporter of the STATESMAN visited Ake at the police station, but he refused to give the name of his dead companion. The clothes of each of the men were thoroughly wet, and both drunk.
ike-johnson-1882-01-02.A4:
JEFF AKES INTERVIEWED IN
THE JAIL.
WHAT HE HAD TO SAY
ABOUT THE MATTER.
THE DEAD MAN BURRIED I
THE CEMETERY.
Yesterday at 9 o'clock Justice Gregg called the jury of inquest, in the case of the man killed in the first ward Monday night, and a thorough and searching investigation as to the facts governing the killing was had. The evidence in the case is, in substance, just about what was stated in yesterday's STATESMAN, and is as follows:

THE EVIDENCE.

Captain J. L. Watts, being sworn, testified: Last night about 11 o'clock I was informed, while on duty, that two white men had assaulted a colored man near Bertram's store, and that the unknown parties had gone towards the first ward. I went with the colored man that way, looking for the men, and came upon them in a house of ill-fame, known as Sallie Daggett's. Two heres were hitched in front, and recognized as the horses ridden by the men. I had a full description of the men. As I came to the gate I met Billie McCllan, and when inside I asked him to assist me in the arrest. Two of the girls, upon inquiry, said the men in question were in the wine room. I then crossed the little platform in the rear, leading to the said wine room, and met the two men aforesaid. I, approaching them, took each by the arm, saying: "Gentlemen, consider yourselves under arrest." Instantly both jumped back, drawing their pistols. I knocked the deceased off the steps, he having a pistol in his hand, and whirling to grab the other, one Jeff Ake, now present, the latter fired at me, striking me in the side. We began wrestling, and I observed the deceased again on his feet and advancing, aiming his pistol at me with both hands. I hallowed to McCllan, "For God's sake kill him!" He (McC.) said he had no pistol, and, upon my request, quickly took mine from my belt, as I could not get away from Jeff Ake. McCllan fired upon the deceased. When I succeeded in getting Jeff Ake to the door and throwing him I learned from McCllan that the deceased was shot. The prisoner had fired a second shot, ineffectually, at me, while the tussle was continuing. Upon the appearance of the city marshal, in answer to summons through others, coming upon the scene, I left with Jeff Ake in custody. Above happened on 2nd day of January, A. D., 1883.

J. L. Watts.

R. J. Stewart, being sworn, testifies: When I came into the hall, Officer Watts had a man down, and one McClellan was standing near by, who said shut the door and don't let anybody in. He further said, there might be some more of them, and, that one was down outside, and he thought was dying. During this Officer Watts still held Jeff Ake down. After shutting the door, I went out through the back door and found the deceased lying on the gallery in a dying condition, and I remained as policeman to keep the crowd up, until the marshal arrived. The doctor came, and Officer Watts left with Jeff Ake. I heard firing, and went to see what was the matter.

R. J. STEWART.

Ike Johnson, being sworn, testifies: Last night near eleven o'clock, I was going home, near Bertram's old store, with my wife, and met two white men in the road, and to keep from being run over, I gave the road, saying, to Jeff Ake, who I now recognize as the man, "Look out, mister, this may cost you something." He rode on a piece, wheeling and coming back, taking out their pistols, and throwing them in my face. The prisoner threw his pistol on me, and the deceased on my wife.

I kept driving, they saying to my wife and myself several times, and making us repeat in the affirmative, "didn't we like it." Jeff Ake then lashed my horse with a buggy whip. Jeff Ake said his name was something like Henry Roundtree, and the deceased, that his was Garfield, and asked us didn't we know them, and other loud and offensive language. They turned suddenly and galloped up the street. On going to inform the officers I met the same men down town, and was intercepted by them, but dodging, tried to cut them off from Mexico, and got Officer Watts, and we went together, as the latter has testified. I was fully able to describe the men and their horses, and gave Captain Watts their description.

AN INTERVIEW WITH JEFF AKES IN JAIL.

A STATESMAN reporter called at the jail yesterday afternoon at 5 o'clock, and requested an interview with Jeff Akes, when Captain A. Denny, the efficient keeper of the prison, courteously showed him up to the cell where the prisoner is confined.

HIS APPEARANCH.

The prisoner is a man of probably thirty-five years of age, five feet six inches high, rather sparely made, and has light or sandy hair. His eye is dull and uninteresting, but the whole contour of his face, as well as his decided expression and precise manner, would seem to indicate decision of character. In fact, his very looks betoken a "bad man," when aroused or under the influence of drink. When informed that a reporter wished to see him, Akes, who was reclining upon a pallet upon the floor, slowly and deliberately arose, seemingly indifferent as to whether he got up or not. His manner toward the interviewer, however, was very civil and might even be called pleasant. His replies to interrogatories put to him were prompt and, apparently, without reservation. He denied most emphatically that he attacked the negro man as stated, and accounts for the assertion upon the theory that he was mistaken for some one else.

HIS STORY

of the fight is to the effect that he and his companion were drinking, and visited the house where the difficulty occurred simply "upon a lark." He says that when Mr. Watts approached him he did not know he (Watts) was an officer, and had he been duly apprised of the fact no resistance would have been made. He also said the officer put his hand upon his pistol, which caused him to draw and fire. He says he only shot once, and thought he was acting in self-defense.

THE DEAD MAN'S IDENTITY.

According to the testimony of Akes, the young man killed lived at or near Bonham, in Fannin county, and had a mother, brother and two sisters in that section. He had been working for the prisoner (Akes) for some time, but had quit the place. He fur-

The prisoner has, or purposely assumes,

Jeff Ake, the man concerned in the recent killing in this city, and the one who fired the shot that struck officer Watts, was yesterday released on bond and is now at liberty. He was held under three charges, and his aggregated bail bonds amount to $1,100, his surety in all three cases being Mr. W. M. Hill, of Williamson county. john-adams-big-valley-1882-02-24.A2:
TEEY MEANT BUSINESS.
It is learned from C. A. McCash, a resident of Adir, Modoc county, who called at this office last evening, that the Vigilantes have been doing some hanging in Big Valley, Lassen county. An old criminal and desperado, by the name of John Adams, a half-breed Mexican, has been hanging around that portion of the country for some time past stealing horses, committing other depressions, and terrorizing the people. That section is very sparsely settled, and the law's protection is a weak arm indeed. The neighbors assembled, held a consultation, and had a committee wait upon him, and ask him to leave that portion of the country. He laughed at the committee, told them there were not enough men in Lassen county to intimidate, nor in the state to hang him. He boldly asserted that he was an outlaw, and recounted many of his thieving exploits in their neighborhood. When the time had elapsed which the committee had given him to make himself scarce, the desperate fellow still remained. The neighbors again assembled last Friday night, and the verdict of all was that he should be lynched. Accordingly they went that night, about 11 o'clock, to where he was known to be stopping, at a house near the banks of Pit river, secreted themselves, some thirty strong, and watched for his appearance. They were not long in waiting, when they saw him passing from the house to the barn. Immediately he was seized by strong and resolute men, bound, conveyed to a convenient oak tree, and with little ceremony John Adams in a few moments was hanging 'by the neck, a lifeless corpse.

For the past three or four days a very stylish young fellow from San Francisco has been in Carson, says the Appeal, frequenting the saloons and talking like a blood. Yesterday afternoon it was discovered that he is a woman. She hurriedly left on the five o'clock train for Virginia.

Wednesday afternoon, says the Eureka Leader, Mrs. Thomas Dixon took hold of the bridle of her husband's horse, that had come home alone, and started to put him in the stable. laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A3:

Bloodshed in Lake County.
OFTLAND. March 12th.—The Oreax
Bloodshed in Lake County.
PORTLAND, March 12th.—The Oregonian's Jacksonville special says: Last night at 10 o'clock ten or twelve masked men rode into Linkville, where A. C. Laws, charged with the murder of Frank Calavan, was in custody of Deputy Sheriff J. F. Lewis and Justice Wright awaiting examination before the latter, which was to take place Monday. The officers were in Greenman's Hotel with the prisoner when the lynchers entered the hall and were ordered to halt. The lynchers refused, and Lewis fired his revolver, wounding one of the party slightly. The lynchers returned the fire, killing the Deputy Sheriff and wounding Justice Wright. They then left without taking Laws. The excitement is intense, and the feeling in Langell valley is very strong against Laws.
laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A4:
LAWLESS DESPERADOES IN LAKE COUNTY.
George Law, who murdered the Calavan boy, on February 13th, about ten miles east of Langell valley, in vicinity of the State line between Modoc and Lake counties, which we mentioned several days ago, is a noted desperado, and chief of the Bonanza Regulators, an organization to prevent settlers from locating in the vicinity of Bonanza. Other persons have been killed suspiciously on former occasions, chargeable to these regulators, who seem to govern that portion of Lake county with as much terror as the cowboys in Arizona. The father of these boys was clubbed sometime ago, and just before an old man was found murdered in his cabin, who had taken up some land for a home. The two boys, when accosted by Law, expected trouble, as threats had been previously made, and the older boy, age 19, had his pistol cocked as quick as Law had his Winchester cocked, both firing instantly, though the younger boy, aged 15, said before his death that Law fired first. Law followed the boys for a fight, as they were not disturbing him, and only looking on the feed grounds for some of their missing cattle. The oldest boy fired his revolver six times at Law, in return for as many rifle shots, and then told his younger brother, who was unarmed, to run his horse at full speed for home, as he had no shots left. As the boy started Law commenced shooting at him, and noticing he was wounded, the older boy sung out to him to let go the bridle rein and hang to the saddle, the latter taking to the brush, as his horse was wounded and unable to travel. The elder Calavan boy felt a bullet pass close by his cheek while in the brush, supposed to be young Law's rifle, and hanging his coat in the brush as a blind he managed to crawl away and escape to his cabin, where the younger brother had pulled off his boots and appeared to be in a dying condition, though able to talk. The elder boy then procured medical assistance from Langell valley, but could not save him. A large posse of citizens, about a dozen or more, headed by the Constable of Bonanza, started to Law's place to arrest him. The Constable thought it best for only three of them to go to Law's place, as he might otherwise show fight. Accordingly they succeeded in making the arrest, but young Law, aged about 20, got the drop on the officer, compelling him to surrender, and, wheeling around quickly, obliged the other two men to do the same. Young Law, assisted by his father and two other persons, after causing the Constable and the two citizens to leave, concluded to follow them, and run them down to where the balance of the citizens were secreted, who, having formed themselves into a circle, succeeded in securing young Law and two other men named Gordon and McKillen, the old man getting away. The elder Law was defiant, and said he would not be taken alive, though it is said he has given himself up, and was bound over by the Bonanza Justice, the others being discharged. There seems to be some doubt whether the murder was committed in Oregon or California. There is a strong feeling against these regulators in both Lake and Modoc counties, and the necks of Law and others will not be safe from Judge Lynch if they can be caught away from their stronghold.—[Yreka Journal, March 8th.

laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A16:
Tragical Tales.
At a dance at the house of John Mooney, in Indian Territory, on the night of the 10th inst., two young men named Montgomery and Horton got into a quarrel, which ended in both drawing pistols and shooting several times at each other. Montgomery was killed outright and Horton mortally wounded.

Two laborers named Monahan and MacAvoy quarreled at Steubenville, O., on the 11th inst. The latter was fatally stabbed.

At Linkville, Oregon, on the night of the 11th inst., a mob of masked men attempted to take a murderer named H. C. Lewis from the jail. Lewis fired on the mob, who responded with a volley, which killed the deputy sheriff and wounded Justice Wright. The would-be lynchers then retired.

A terrible tragedy was enacted at a school house at Harrisburg, Pernsett County, Ark., on the 7th inst. County Treasurer J. J. Smith remonstrated with the teacher for whipping his child. The conversation became heated and finally led to Smith's striking E. J. Wilmot, the teacher, on the head with a billet of wood, crushing his skull. The injured man died in three hours.

In a drunken quarrel at New Orleans on the night of the 7th inst., Richard Shea was stabbed to death by James Cosgrove.

An aged couple named O'Massey, living near Charlottesville, Va., were found murdered on the morning of the 8th inst., in their house. Money was the object.

A mob took Charles Shelton, John Redmond and Harry French from the jail at Los Lunas, Cal., on the 8th inst., and hung them to a tree.

A courtesan named Mary Sigman and her mother were assassinated at Mount Vernon, Ky., on the 8th inst.

A remarkable story comes from the City of Mexico. The report is that highwaymen attacked a stage full of armed men and that eleven of the outlaws were killed.

It is reported that nine Europeans journeying from Tunis to Gafsa were murdered between Tunis and Kairwan.

Advices from New Mexico are to the effect that Deputy Sheriff Miers and Martinez with a posse were attacked by Pueblo Indians while attempting to arrest some of the Pueblos who had escaped from jail. Miers was killed and Martinez mortally wounded.

A shocking tragedy took place at Boston, Mass., on the 7th inst. Mrs. Harriet Bell while returning from a grocery store near her home was accosted by an unknown man who followed her to the doorstep of her home and then cut her throat. She lived but a short time. The assassin escaped.

A brace of cattle thieves named Arnold Howard and Frank Young, in jail at Del Noter, Col., were visited by a mob on the 7th inst. Howard was killed outright and Young mortally wounded.

An affray with pistols took place at Arkansas City, on the 5th inst., in which J. W. Hale was killed by John Fuller.

Three negroes—Lewis Smith and Aaron and Ed. Clark—were killed in an affray at Arkadelphia, Ark., on the 6th inst. The shooting was done by Joe Ross and Thad. Henry, both white.

Tax Collector Robert Taylor was shot dead by Dr. Sims at Perryville, Perry County, Ark., on the 4th inst.

TRIED TO LYNCH HIM.

Justice Wright and Deputy Sheriff Lewis, with several others were in the office. The Lynchers ordered all to sit down, which was obeyed. The leader then took a light from the table, saying, "We want the prisoner. Come on, boys," and weat into the hall. A shot was fired from upstairs by the prisoner's guard about that time. Lewis was then shot by the lynchers through the thigh, cutting the femoral artery, and died five minutes after. The shot extinguished the lights in the office and those present jumped out of the window. Justice Wright was shot in the arm, the bullet grazing his side. The lynchers then left, taking with them a wounded man, who is supposed to be shot in the head, as a hat was picked up riddled with shot and a piece of scalp with a tuft of hair attached. The shot that struck him is supposed to have been fired by Lewis, as a gun was found behind him with one barrel discharged and he had no arms on him.

It is hard to say who fired the first shot in the office. The supposition is that the leaders of the lynchers were from Modoc county, California, where the friends of the boy Calavar, who was murdered by Laws, reside, and that they were reinforced by cattle men from Langell valley and Bonanza. There is no sympathy for Laws, but the killing of Deputy Sheriff Lewis is deeply regretted. laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A22:
DARING DESPERADO.
Laws, the Murderer of Frank Calavan, Resists Arrest and Makes it Lively for the Sheriff.
On the 18th of February an officer left Boiseman, Lake county, says the Jacksonville Sentinel, with a posse of ten citizens to arrest H. C. Law, the murderer of young Calavan. On arriving at Law's house he was found to be absent and nine of the party concealed themselves in the barn. The officer and another man proceeded to Steel's swamp, about seven miles father on, where Lee Law and another young man were feeding cattle. The officer succeeded in arrest them, taking three revolvers from them. they neglected to secure the prisoners, however, and young Law, watching his opportunity, snatched his revolver from the officer and leveling it on him compelled the astonished functionary to return the other two weapons. Young Law then mounted his horse, took one of the pistols to his father and returning gave chase to the officer and his man and drove them on the dead run to the Law ranch. On arriving there the tables were turned on young Law and his companions, the whole posse making their appearance with cocked guns and compelling them to throw up their hands and surrender. The names of the three parties brought in are Lee Law and two young men named Gordon and McKillen, and thought to be the three men who fired on the Calavan boys from the brush when they were trying to escape. The elder Law, who killed young Calavan, is very defiant and says he will not be taken
w o killed young Calavan, is very defiant and says he will not be taken alive. It now remains to be seen whether there are men enough in Lake county to enforce the law. There is pluck enough among the cattie men, and we believe if they find the murderer they will make short work of him if he resists. The latest report is to the effect that H. C. Law has given himself up and was bound over and the other parties discharged.
laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A25:
COAST AND STATE.
Redwood creek and harbor, in San Mateo county, are complaining of the debris filling them up, and asking our uncle to dredge them out.

The Vallejo Odd Fellows have decided to celebrate the coming anniversary of their Order by an excursion on April 26th to Fairfax Park, near San Rafael, in Marin county, and have engaged the steamer San Rafael for the trip.

The San Jose Mercury says: The numerous attempts made during the past three months to burn the churches of this city, one of which at last proved successful, would seem to indicate there is a crank running loose who is greatly in need of a little judicious killing.

Salmon are now beginning to run pretty plentifully, and the run will increase for several weeks. From fifty to a hundred boats are now engaged in the Straits fisheries, catching an average of twenty to thirty salmon a day. A larger number will soon be employed, and the average catch per boat will be larger during the next two months. —[Contra Costa Gazette.

The farmers in the neighborhood of Vallejo and Benicia are much pleased with the present prospects of large crops. The season was so favorable that almost every available acre of land was put in, and if the weather continues favorable a larger crop will be harvested than ever before. On account of so much land being sown with grain the hay crop will be very short, and it is thought that some of the grain will have to be cut for hay.

The Lakeview (Or.) Examiner says that the men who composed the mob that attempted to lynch Laws at Linkville, and in the melee killed Deputy Sheriff Lewis, are all Lassen county men, and live in and around Beiber and Big Valley. The Examiner gives a detailed account of the fracas, which, if true, shows that the lynchers acted in a cowardly and cold-blooded manner. They all broke and ran for the brush after killing an officer who was powerless in their hands, he at the time he was shot crouching down under cover of a mobber's shotgun.

A meeting of the Seattle, Puget Sound and Gray's Harbor Railroad and Transportation Company was held in Seattle. The President, Governor Newell, and other members of the Board were present. A report was received from the engineer who had made a survey over the proposed route, which represented that the grading and trestle work would be comparatively small. The location of termini on Puget Sound and harbor were not definitely settled. Steilacoom, Johnson's, Dofflamyer's and Brown's points and Olympia were carefully discussed, but no conclusion reached. The road will be about fifty miles in length, passing through one of the very best and most extensive regions of fir, cedar and spruce timber in Washington Territory, along the valley of the Chehalis, well known as one of the most fertile valleys of the Sound country, already highly cultivated and thickly inhabited. It was resolved unanimously to press the enterprise vigorously, and, if possible, to secure an early construction of the road.
laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A26: The people of Lakeview are determined to try and secure the arrest of persons connected with the mob at Linkville. The Commissioners have offered $1,000 reward, and the citizens intend subscribing another $1,000 to secure at least two or more. Should that many be found, it is believed the rest may be found out, all of whom will no doubt be indicted for the murder of Deputy Sheriff Lewis. The Oregonians claim that the mob comprised Californians from Big Valley, and the Big Valley people say they were friends of Laws endeavoring to get Laws from custody under pretense of desiring to lynch him. The latter charge, however, is not generally believed, but it is a matter of doubt whether the mob consisted of Oregonians or Californians, and may have comprised both, as Laws was a terror to the people along the boundary line, where several murders committed are charged to him and the Bonanza regulators, of which organization he was the chief.—[Yreka Journal.
laws-linkville-1882-03-11.A28:
A Travetsy on Justice.
For some cause the grand jury of Moloc county, Cal., did not find an indictment against H. C. Laws, who killed young Calavan near the State line sometime since. This is a surprise and has occasioned a deal of public indignation.
